# Logistic Regression {#sec-ch09}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

knitr::read_chunk("../r_companion/scripts/chapter_09.R")
# Wrap R's printed output to fit the page.
options(width = 68)
```

This chapter fits the logistic regression models from [Chapter 9 of the textbook](../chapters/chapter-09.html) and gets the values the textbook uses to judge them: odds ratios with confidence intervals, VIF, predicted probabilities, deviance $R^2$, the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, a confusion matrix, and an ROC curve with its AUC. The function is `glm()`, which works almost exactly like `lm()` from Chapters 4 and 5.

**Get the script:** [Download the Chapter 9 script, `chapter_09.R`](scripts/chapter_09.R), and save it in the same folder as your data.

## The data

[Download `youth_risk_2007.csv`](../data/youth_risk_2007.csv) into the same folder as the script. It holds answers from 13,387 high school students to the 2007 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which you used in Chapter 2. The question in this chapter: which students are more likely to have tried smoking?

The variables used in this chapter:

| Variable | Type | What it records |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `smoke` | Categorical | Lifetime tobacco experimentation indicator ($1 = \text{yes, has tried smoking cigarettes (even a few puffs)}$, $0 = \text{no}$). |
| `ride.alc.driver` | Categorical | Riding with a Drunk Driver (RDD) indicator within the past 30 days ($1 = \text{yes, rode with a driver who had been drinking}$, $0 = \text{no}$). |
| `age4` | Categorical | The respondent's age in years, restricted to adolescent age brackets (**14**, **15**, **16**, **17**, or **18** years old). |

: Variables from `youth_risk_2007.csv` used in this chapter {tbl-colwidths="[23,17,60]"}

`age4` holds ages in whole years, so the models below use it as a number: each slope is the change for one more year of age.

## Load the packages and the data

This chapter uses four packages: `ggplot2` for the ROC curve's look, `car` for VIF, `pROC` for the ROC curve and its AUC, and `DescTools` for the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. If any is not installed yet, go back to [Install and load packages](chapter-00.qmd#sec-packages) in Getting Set Up.

```{r load-packages}
```

::: {.callout-note title="Messages when car and pROC load"}
`car` loads its companion package of example datasets, as in Chapter 5. `pROC` prints a citation note and says that some of its functions are "masked from 'package:stats'." That means `pROC` has its own versions of three functions with the same names. Nothing in this companion uses them, so you can ignore the message.
:::

```{r read-data}
```

The outcome is coded 0 and 1, as logistic regression needs, and 388 students did not answer the question (`<NA>`).

::: {.callout-warning title="Common error: y values must be 0 <= y <= 1"}
**What you see**

```{r}
#| error: true
pressure <- read.csv("smoking_bmi_bp.csv")
glm(Smoker ~ BMI, data = pressure, family = binomial)
```

**What it means:** the outcome is stored as words (`Yes` and `No`), not as 0 and 1.

**How to fix it:** create a 0/1 version of the outcome with `ifelse()` from Chapter 8, with 1 for the event you are predicting, and use the new column in `glm()`:

```r
pressure$SmokerYes <- ifelse(pressure$Smoker == "Yes", 1, 0)
```
:::

## Simple logistic regression

`glm()` takes the outcome before the `~` and the predictor after it, like `lm()`. Two extra arguments make it a logistic regression that handles missing values:

```{r simple}
```

The `Coefficients` table has the same columns as [the textbook's Table 9.1](../chapters/chapter-09.html#interpreting-the-output-slopes-and-odds-ratios), apart from the odds ratios, which come next. Read it in two steps:

1. **The slope's sign and p-value.** The `Estimate` for `age4` is 0.237, a log-odds slope: positive, so older students were more likely to have tried smoking, *p* < .001.
2. **The odds ratio.** `exp(coef())` turns each slope into an odds ratio. For `age4` it is 1.267: each extra year of age multiplies the odds of having tried smoking by 1.27, a 26.7% increase in the odds. Ignore the `(Intercept)` odds ratio.

The line `(439 observations deleted due to missingness)` tells you how many students were left out because they were missing the outcome or the predictor.

::: {.callout-note title="Check: the family line"}
Look for `(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)` near the bottom of the output. If it says `gaussian` instead, you left out `family = binomial`, and R fit an ordinary regression without any error or warning. Add the argument and run the model again.
:::

## Graph the probability curve

A graph shows what the model predicts at every age. It puts each student's answer (0 or 1) on a scatterplot, then draws the predicted probability as a curve with its 95% confidence band:

```{r curve}
#| fig-cap: "Each student's answer by age, with the fitted probability curve and its 95% confidence band."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of having tried smoking against age, from 14 to 18 years, for 12,948 students. Faint gray dots form two horizontal rows, one at 1 for students who had tried smoking and one at 0 for students who had not, each split into five patches, one per age; the patches at ages 14 and 18 are lighter because fewer students were those ages. A blue curve rises almost in a straight line from a probability of 0.41 at age 14 to 0.64 at age 18. A shaded 95% confidence band surrounds the curve but is so narrow it is barely wider than the line."
```

The faint dots along the top are students who had tried smoking (1), and the dots along the bottom are students who had not (0); the darker a patch of dots, the more students it holds, so ages 14 and 18 look lighter only because fewer students were those ages. The curve rises from a probability of 0.41 at age 14 to 0.64 at age 18. The band is so narrow it is barely wider than the line, because almost 13,000 students went into the model; with a smaller sample, it would be much wider.

The graph also shows what the slope means. The log-odds slope (0.237) and the odds ratio (1.27) are the same for every extra year of age, but the probability does not rise by a fixed amount each year. A logistic curve is [an S shape](../chapters/chapter-09.html#the-core-concept-moving-beyond-2x2-tables), steepest at a probability of 0.50 and flattening toward 0 and 1. Ages 14 to 18 cover only the middle of the S, where it is nearly straight, so each year here adds about 6 percentage points (5.8 from 14 to 15, and 5.6 from 17 to 18). If a predictor pushed the probabilities close to 0 or 1, the same odds ratio would add much less probability per unit near the ends.

::: {.callout-tip title="With your own data"}
Change the dataset and the variables in `subset()`, the predictor's name and range in `data.frame()`, the model's name in `predict()`, and the variable names, title, and labels in `ggplot()`. Keep the range inside your data, so the curve does not extrapolate. For a predictor with many different values, such as income, set `width = 0` in `position_jitter()` so the dots stay at their real values.
:::

## Multiple logistic regression

List the predictors after the `~`, joined with `+` signs, as in Chapter 5:

```{r multiple}
```

Both predictors are significant, *p* < .001, each while holding the other constant. For the odds ratios with their 95% confidence intervals, in the layout of [the textbook's Table 9.4](../chapters/chapter-09.html#interpreting-the-odds-ratios):

```{r odds-ratios}
```

- **`ride.alc.driver`:** students who had ridden with a driver who had been drinking had 3.18 times the odds of having tried smoking, 95% CI [2.94, 3.45], compared with students of the same age who had not.
- **`age4`:** each extra year of age multiplies the odds by 1.26 (a 26% increase), 95% CI [1.22, 1.30], for students with the same answer about riding with a drinking driver.

```{r vif}
```

Both VIFs are 1.00, so the predictors do not overlap.

::: {.callout-note title="confint() or confint.default()?"}
`confint.default()` gives Wald intervals, the kind most statistics programs report (and the textbook uses). You may see `confint()` in other R guides. It uses a different method that refits the model many times to find each interval's ends; the message `Waiting for profiling to be done...` only means R is doing that work. Its intervals are a little more accurate in small samples. With a large sample, the two agree closely; use `confint.default()` to match the textbook.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="With your own data"}
Change the outcome, the predictors, the dataset, and the model's name. Use the model's name in the odds ratio and VIF lines too. A categorical predictor stored as words works as in Chapter 5: R makes the indicator variables and names each row after its group.
:::

## Predicted probabilities

To predict the probability for specific people, build a small table of profiles with `data.frame()`. It needs one column for each predictor, named exactly as in the model:

```{r predict}
```

A 16-year-old who had not ridden with a drinking driver has a predicted probability of 0.44 (44%) of having tried smoking; a 16-year-old who had has a probability of 0.72 (72%). The `1` and `2` above the probabilities are the row numbers of the profiles.

::: {.callout-tip title="With your own data"}
Give `data.frame()` one column per predictor, using the predictor names from your model, and list one value per profile inside each `c()`. Every column needs the same number of values. For a categorical predictor stored as words, type the group name in quotes, such as `Group = c("Control", "Treatment")`.
:::

## Deviance R-squared

R does not print the deviance $R^2$, but it stores the pieces needed to calculate it. The first line gives the deviance $R^2$, and the second the adjusted deviance $R^2$:

```{r deviance-r2}
```

The model reduced the deviance by 6.1% compared with a model with no predictors (adjusted deviance $R^2$ also 6.1%, since the sample is large). The predictors are significant, but they leave most of the deviance unexplained, [the same pattern the textbook describes for its ICU model](../chapters/chapter-09.html#deviance-r2-and-adjusted-deviance-r2).

## Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test

The Hosmer-Lemeshow test sorts the people into groups by their predicted probability and compares how many 1s each group actually had with how many the model predicted. Some software also reports a deviance goodness-of-fit test, but its p-value is unreliable when each combination of predictor values belongs to only a few people; grouping lets Hosmer-Lemeshow hold up in that situation. As the textbook explains, [its hypotheses run backward](../chapters/chapter-09.html#the-hosmer-lemeshow-goodness-of-fit-test): a large p-value means you have no evidence that the model fits poorly.

```{r hosmer-lemeshow}
```

The result: $\chi^2(6) = 12.72$, *p* = .048. Taken alone, that p-value is just below .05, evidence that the model does not fit well.

::: {.callout-note title="Warning: Found only 8 different groups"}
The test normally uses 10 groups. This model has only two predictors with few values (0 or 1, and five ages), so it gives only 10 different predicted probabilities, and some of them are too close together to split into 10 groups. R uses the 8 groups it can make, lowers the degrees of freedom to match (8 − 2 = 6), and tells you so. The warning does not mean anything went wrong. (The misspelling "Hosmer-Lemesho" is R's.)
:::

### A large sample makes small differences significant

Before you conclude that the model fits badly, look at how big the differences are. The first line gives the share of students in each group who actually had tried smoking, and the second the share the model predicted:

```{r hosmer-lemeshow-groups}
```

Each label is the range of predicted probabilities in that group, such as `(0.499,0.556]` for students the model gave a 50% to 56% chance. In every group, the model's prediction is within about 4 percentage points of what happened (for example, 0.53 actual and 0.56 predicted in the fourth group). With 12,948 students, the test is powerful enough to call even differences this small significant. This is [the textbook's warning about sample size and practical significance](../chapters/chapter-03.html#the-limitation-of-the-p-value): a p-value measures the strength of the evidence, not the size of the problem. With a large sample, report the test, and judge the fit by comparing the two lines as well.

::: {.callout-tip title="With your own data"}
Change the model's name in both places in the `HosmerLemeshowTest()` line. If your model has a continuous predictor (as the textbook's ICU model has age), you will get the full 10 groups and 8 degrees of freedom, and no warning.
:::

## Confusion matrix

`fitted()` gives each student's predicted probability. Store it as a new column, turn it into a 0/1 prediction with a 50% threshold, and cross-tabulate the predictions against what actually happened:

```{r confusion}
```

At the 50% threshold, the model's sensitivity is 0.52 (it caught 52% of the students who had tried smoking) and its specificity is 0.71 (it correctly identified 71% of those who had not). [To try a different threshold](../chapters/chapter-09.html#adjusting-the-threshold), as the textbook describes, change the `0.5` in the `ifelse()` line and run the lines below it again.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common error: replacement has 12948 rows, data has 13387"}
**What you see**

```{r}
#| error: true
no_exclude <- glm(smoke ~ ride.alc.driver + age4, data = youth,
                  family = binomial)
youth$prob <- fitted(no_exclude)
```

**What it means:** without `na.action = na.exclude`, the model leaves out the rows with missing values completely, so it has fewer predictions than the dataset has rows.

**How to fix it:** add `na.action = na.exclude` inside `glm()` and fit the model again. The missing rows then get `NA` as their prediction, and the column fits.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common error: subscript out of bounds"}
**What you see**

```{r}
#| error: true
strict <- table(Predicted = ifelse(youth$prob > 0.9, 1, 0),
                Actual = youth$smoke)
strict
strict["1", "1"] / sum(strict[, "1"])
```

**What it means:** no student has a predicted probability over 0.9, so every prediction is 0 and the table has no row named `1`. The same thing happens at the 50% threshold when the outcome is rare or very common, as with the textbook's ICU model, where nearly everyone is predicted to survive.

**How to fix it:** print the confusion matrix before calculating. If it has only one row, the rule never predicts the other outcome; try a threshold closer to the middle of the predicted probabilities.
:::

## ROC curve and AUC

`roc()` compares the actual outcomes with the predicted probabilities at every possible threshold, and `auc()` gives the area under the curve:

```{r roc}
```

The AUC is 0.66. On [the common grading scale](../chapters/chapter-09.html#grading-the-model-area-under-the-curve-auc), that is above 0.50 (guessing) but below the 0.70 that counts as acceptable.

::: {.callout-note title="Messages: Setting levels and Setting direction"}
`roc()` reports which outcome it treated as the event (`case = 1`) and that the event should have the higher predicted probabilities. Both are what you want for a 0/1 outcome, so you can ignore the messages.
:::

Draw the ROC curve with `ggroc()`, which makes a ggplot:

```{r roc-plot}
#| fig-cap: "ROC curve for the logistic regression of ever smoking on riding with a drinking driver and age."
#| fig-alt: "ROC curve with the false positive rate along the bottom and sensitivity up the side, both from 0 to 1. A solid curve bows up and to the left of a dashed diagonal line that runs from the lower left corner to the upper right. The curve stays modestly above the diagonal the whole way, matching an AUC of 0.66."
```

The curve bows above the dashed "coin flip" diagonal, but not far toward the top-left corner, which matches the modest AUC.

::: {.callout-tip title="With your own data"}
Put your outcome and your predicted probability column inside `roc()`, then change the name inside `auc()` and `ggroc()`, and update the title.
:::
